questions.q: Which of these should you do BEFORE building any clever model?
options: Deploy to production
Tune hyperparameters on the test set
Define the metric and set a simple baseline
Add as many features as possible
questions.explain: Framing the problem, choosing a metric and establishing a baseline come first, so you know what a good result looks like.

questions.q: A dataset is 63% benign and 37% malignant. A model that always predicts benign scores about what accuracy?
options: About 37%
About 63%
About 100%
About 50%
questions.explain: Always guessing the majority class scores the majority share, about 63%. That is the baseline any real model has to beat.

questions.q: Why are models fitted on X_train only and scored on X_test?
options: Scikit-learn refuses to fit on more than 75% of the data
Training data is always cleaner
It makes fitting faster
Scoring on rows the model has seen would give a flattering, dishonest estimate
questions.explain: The test rows stand in for future unseen data. Scoring on training rows overstates how well the model will do in the real world.

questions.q: You try ten models and choose whichever scores best on the test set. What is the problem?
options: The test score is no longer an honest estimate, because you indirectly tuned against it
Ten models is too few
Nothing, this is the standard method
The test set will be deleted
questions.explain: Repeated selection on the test set leaks it into your choices. Experiments belong on a validation set, and the test set is used once at the end.

questions.q: Which statement about the ML workflow is most accurate?
options: It is a straight line that ends when the model is trained
Modeling is the largest step and data work is minor
Deployment is the end, with nothing to monitor
It is a loop: evaluation often sends you back to data preparation or problem framing
questions.explain: Poor evaluation typically leads back to better features, more data or a reframed problem, and deployed models need monitoring for drift.
